note: Vol. II No. 7. The masthead prints 'Wednesday June 4 1835' although June 4 was a Thursday, and corpus.json records the printed wording. The land sale of 15 June is now eleven days off and the issue is bent around it: a leading article on pre-emption customs, C. C. Van Horn coming to town 'from the 25th until after the land sale', and a prices current in which superfine flour has doubled in eight days. THE FORT ADVERTISES FOR ITS OWN SUPPLIES for the first time in this range — beef for a year, five hundred cords of wood by kind, and twenty tons of prairie hay — which is the most concrete thing this corpus has on what Fort Dearborn consumed.

THE TOWN RUNS OUT OF FOOD, ELEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE LAND SALE. Flour at twelve dollars a barrel — and the prices current on page 3 of this same issue quotes superfine at $10.00-12.00, against $5.00-6.50 eight days earlier. The editorial and the table agree, which is what makes the figure usable: one is the editor's ear and the other is the weekly quotation, and they were set on the same day.

'ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE TO OBTAIN […] AT ANY PRICE' IS THE STRONGER CLAIM. A market that has run out is not a market with a high price, and by 1835-06-24 superfine flour is quoted at $15.00-16.00 — tripled in a month. The cause is stated in the same sentence: consumption, not failure of supply. Chicago's population in the weeks before the scene date was rising faster than its provisioning, and 1835-06-17 supplies the corroborating image of 'the immense congregation of strangers crowding every room of our public houses'.

The transcription is interleaved with an adjacent column and the left edge of every line is clipped; the bracketed supplies are the minimum for sense and none of them touches a figure.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO A RECONSTRUCTION. The materials block is a stable, weekly-quoted price series for the exact months being modelled, and its stability across a food panic is evidence that the building trade was supplied — lumber was arriving, brick was being made or landed, lime was in barrels. A town that cannot feed itself and can still buy brick at six dollars a thousand is building fast, which is what 'whichever way we turn our eyes they encounter new buildings' (1835-05-20) says in words.

WHAT IT IS CALLED CHANGES, AND THE CHANGE IS THE EVIDENCE. This printing and 1835-06-10 say 'John H. Kinzie's new building'; 1835-06-24 says 'J. H. Kinzie's new store'. So the building is a STORE with lettable office space in it, which is the same species as the 20-by-45 store with three office rooms Kinzie was letting in Kinzie's Addition in October 1834 (1835-05-20) — and MAY OR MAY NOT BE THE SAME STRUCTURE. It is not fused here: the 1834 notice calls its store finished and this one calls Moore's new, eight months later, and John H. Kinzie was building more than one thing in these years. NO STREET is named in any printing, so nothing is placed; what is established is that a new Kinzie commercial building existed and had a lawyer in it at the scene date.

The reference to Joseph Story of Cambridge is a Massachusetts credential and places nothing here.

claims.notes:
FIVE HUNDRED CORDS OF WOOD AND TWENTY TONS OF PRAIRIE HAY, SPECIFIED BY SPECIES, DIMENSION AND CUTTING DATE. This is the richest single piece of material evidence in the eight issues and every clause of it is usable.

THE SPECIES LIST IS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE COUNTRY AROUND CHICAGO: white oak, hickory, white ash and maple, 'and no other'. The army would not specify four hardwoods and refuse everything else unless a contractor could actually deliver five hundred cords of them within hauling distance in one season. That is a hard constraint on what the timber belt held, and it is independent of every map-derived and botanical source this project has used.

THE CORD IS DEFINED — 8 feet long, 4 feet high, 4 feet wide, 'from half the slope of each end of the stick' — which is the standard 128 cubic feet, stated. Five hundred of them is 64,000 cubic feet of firewood for one garrison for one winter, stacked 'at such place near Fort Dearborn as will be designated'. A woodyard of that size beside the fort is a visible feature and nothing in the reconstruction has one.

THE HAY IS CUT IN JULY. Twenty tons of prairie hay, 'to be cut in July or before the 10th of August next', 2000 pounds to the ton by actual weight. The scene date is 1 July 1835: the haying this notice buys begins in the modelled month, on the prairie, for the fort's animals.

The advertisement is interleaved with two others and `lines_of_claim` names only its own lines; the wood figure '[8] feet' is supplied from the 1835-06-10 printing, which sets '8 feet long' cleanly where this one prints a broken glyph.

claims.notes:
THE TOWN'S MOOD ELEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE LAND SALE, and it is anxious. The editor is warning incomers not to bid over squatters on land the squatters have improved, and he warns them in the language of a threat — 'public opinion is stronger than law' — and 'for the peace and quietness of our town'. That is a claim jumper's warning printed in the town's only paper, and it says the sale of 15 June 1835 was expected to be contentious enough to need one.

WHY IT BELONGS IN THIS CORPUS. The pre-emption customs it describes are the mechanism by which improvements on the ground — a cabin, a fence, a broken field — converted into title, which is the legal substrate under every inferred household the reconstruction places outside the platted blocks. The paper states plainly that settlers located on UNSURVEYED land and that custom and federal acts had sanctioned it. Nothing here places anything; it is the rule the placements were made under.

The column is clipped at both edges throughout and the supplies are the minimum for sense; no name, date or figure is supplied.

claims.notes:
WHAT WENT INTO CHICAGO'S WINDOWS IN JUNE 1835, argued in the advertisement itself: CROWN glass, said to beat Boston crown for clearness, transparency and strength, and 'cheaper and stronger than cylinder' glass. Crown glass is spun, so it is thicker at the centre and carries the bullion; cylinder glass is blown and flattened and is flatter and more even. A dealer arguing FOR crown against cylinder in this town in this month is direct evidence that both were on sale and that crown was the one being pushed. J. S. C. Hogan's standing advertisement gives the pane sizes — 8 by 10 and 7 by 9, with sash — and between them the two notices describe the glazing of the modelled town about as well as it can be described from paper.

THE ADVERTISEMENT IS BADLY SHREDDED HERE; the bracketed supplies come from the 1835-06-10 printing (lines 2565-2574), which sets the whole notice legibly, and every supply is a word this pass can point at in that printing. Philo Carpenter also advertises quinine by the hundred bottles and ready made clothing in the same column — a druggist with a general consignment trade, unplaced in any printing.
